name: Amira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at Mount Selwyn, the iron ore mine up on the plateau. My job is keeping the haul roads smooth, so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres, which cost more than my house. I start at six with a pre-start check, then I'm up and down the same eight kilometres of road all day, cutting the ruts, spreading the gravel, and the water cart comes behind me. It's satisfying when a road is perfect. The tiring part is the concentration, because a 200-tonne truck coming the other way doesn't brake for you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Viktor and I had a café on Market Street for fifteen years. When the mine had its big downturn a few years back, half the town stopped buying coffee and we went under. We still owe the bank for the coffee machine and the fit-out, so there's not much left over, maybe a couple of weeks of bills in savings. Viktor drives a delivery van now and I came here at fifty-four, which is three, nearly four years ago. I'm still not quick on the grader, but I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's good news for people like us, who don't need more surprises. I'd probably say at break that the computer people got excited over nothing. Online I mostly share recipes, so I'd leave it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I get time, which is what I need most. I'm not fast, but every month nothing changes is a month I get better and the café loan gets smaller. That's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep paying the loan, the way we planned. I'd ask my supervisor, Joe, to let me do the steeper ramps more often so I learn them. Maybe I'd start a little weekend catering again in a year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you might restart catering. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small things, birthday cakes, trays of pastries for funerals and christenings. I used the AI on my phone last month to work out how much to charge, and it was quite helpful, actually. Just enough to put a hundred a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that would still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The autonomous trucks, a bit. They've got some running on the west roads already. But they still need someone to keep the roads good for them, maybe even better, because a robot truck doesn't like a pothole. So in a way they need me more.

S0.say: She'd say a plateau is good news for people who don't need more surprises and that the computer people got excited over nothing.
S0.think: She thinks it gives her time, which she needs most: each month without change is a month she gets better and the café loan shrinks.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying off the café loan as planned. Asks to work the steeper ramps more to improve, and considers restarting weekend catering in about a year.
S0.quote: I'm not fast, but every month nothing changes is a month I get better and the café loan gets smaller.
S0.fieldNote: Amira measures time in loan payments and skill gains, so a plateau is simply more runway. She's a cautious occasional AI user who found it handy for pricing catering work. She even reasons that self-driving trucks might need good roads, and so need her more.

steps.text: Keep grading the Mount Selwyn haul roads and paying the café loan
Ask supervisor Joe for more turns on the steeper ramps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be sensible, find out what the company plans and make a plan of our own. I'm not one for shouting. I'd say it at the crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think graders get automated not long after the trucks. Once you have robot trucks on the roads, a robot grader is the obvious next step. I spent fifteen years watching the coffee machine, now I'd spend my last working years watching my grader drive off without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask in the first month whether there'll be training for the automated graders and put my name down. I'd restart the catering right away instead of waiting, so we have a second income. And we'd try to pay off the café loan faster, even if it means no holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can manage it, but it's there every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for training. How do you feel about learning those systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not the first person to try things, but once I see others doing it, I'm alright. My niece showed me how to use the AI for the catering and I picked it up. If two or three of the others are doing the automation course and it's working, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about Viktor in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Delivery vans, that's another job everyone says will go. If he lost his and I lost mine in the same few years, we'd be back where we were when the café closed. That's my real nightmare, both at once.

S1.say: She'd say people need to be sensible, find out the company's plans and make their own, raising it calmly at the crew meeting.
S1.think: She believes graders will be automated soon after the trucks, and imagines her grader driving off without her as the café machine did.
S1.do: Puts her name down for automated grader training in the first month, once she sees colleagues doing it. Restarts the catering business immediately and pays the café loan faster, skipping holidays.
S1.quote: I spent fifteen years watching the coffee machine, now I'd spend my last working years watching my grader drive off without me.
S1.fieldNote: Amira's worry has two parts, her job and Viktor's delivery van going at once, which echoes the café closure. Her 'once others have' attitude shows clearly: she'd train if colleagues were already doing it successfully. Her first move is a second income, not a protest.

steps.text: Put her name down for automated grader training once others have tried it
Restart weekend catering right away as a second income
Pay off the café loan faster and skip the holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the hands. That's the year Viktor's van and my grader go together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the crew meeting I'd say we have three years before the machines can do our work, so let's find out the company's plan now and make our own. I'd say it calmly. I'm not one for shouting, and shouting wouldn't change the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking machines in 2028 don't touch my grader much, maybe the planning of which road to cut. But in 2031 the robots come for the grader and for Viktor's delivery van in the same year, and that's my nightmare, both at once. I'd be sixty-three, with the pension still a couple of years off and maybe still owing the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare cent on the café loan, plus about two hundred a month from catering, to clear it before 2031. I'd restart the weekend catering straight away, and use the AI on my phone for the orders and prices, because by 2028 it'll be good at that. And I'd go to the council in the first year to ask what help there is for older workers, before we're desperate, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, but with a list. I'd sleep badly, but I'd get up and do the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go to the council before you need help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the café closed, we waited until the bank letters came, and by then every office had a queue. I learned that the hard way. This time I'd want my name on whatever list there is while the queue is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the catering be enough if both jobs went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not by itself. Birthday cakes and funeral trays won't pay a mortgage on a café that doesn't exist. But a hundred a week from the catering would keep the lights on while we work out the rest.

S2.say: We have three years before the machines can do our work, so let's find out the company's plan now and make our own. Shouting wouldn't change the date.
S2.think: The thinking machines in 2028 barely touch my grader, but in 2031 the robots come for the grader and Viktor's van in the same year. I'd be sixty-three, with the pension a couple of years off and maybe still owing the bank.
S2.do: Puts every spare cent and about two hundred a month from catering onto the café loan to clear it before 2031. Restarts weekend catering straight away with the phone AI handling orders and prices, and goes to the council in year one to ask about help for older workers.
S2.feel: Scared but organised. She'd sleep badly, then get up and work through her list.
S2.quote: Birthday cakes and funeral trays won't pay a mortgage on a café that doesn't exist.
S2.fieldNote: Amira saw at once that the three-year gap lands both her grader job and her partner's van job in the same year, which is the outcome she fears most. Her plan is to clear the old café loan before then and get on the council's list early. She learned from the café closing that waiting for the letters costs you.

steps.text: Put every spare cent and catering money on the café loan before 2031
Restart weekend catering now, using the phone AI for orders and prices
Ask the council in year one about help for older workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be sixty-six. That's past the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the crew meeting this is the sensible one, there's time to plan properly. Let the company say what it's doing and we'll do the same. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd make it. The robot graders and the robot vans come in 2034, and I'd be retiring around then anyway. If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing, and that changes everything for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put about two hundred a month of catering money onto the loan for three years. I'd take the automated grader course once the first group reports back, so I'm useful in the last years. After the loan's cleared, I'd start saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a plan I can see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Viktor in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be sixty-five in 2034, so he'd be right at the edge too. It would be close for both of us, but close is better than over. We'd make it if nothing else breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the thinking machines in 2031 change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the catering. The AI would do the ordering and the pricing better than me. I'd let it, and spend my time on the pastries, which is the part people pay for.

S3.say: This is the sensible one, there's time to plan properly. Let the company say what it's doing and we'll do the same.
S3.think: I think I'd make it, because the robot graders and vans come in 2034, around when I'd retire anyway. If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing.
S3.do: Puts about two hundred a month of catering money onto the café loan for three years. Takes the automated grader course once the first group reports back, and starts saving once the loan is cleared.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, with a plan she can see the end of.
S3.quote: If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing, and that changes everything for me.
S3.fieldNote: With robots due in 2034, both Amira and her partner reach retirement right at the edge, which turns her fear into a manageable plan. Her steady approach shows in waiting for the first group to report back before taking the grader course. She'd let AI take the business side of catering and keep the baking.

steps.text: Put about two hundred a month of catering money on the café loan
Keep the weekend catering going, with AI doing orders and pricing
Take the automated grader course once the first group reports back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and thirteen. I'd be retired well before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's fine for people my age and a warning for the young ones. At the crew meeting I'd tell the young ones to learn the new systems early. I'd say it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview. My worry would be the town after we're gone. If the mine runs itself, who buys coffee?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the café loan in the first three years, then save for retirement. I'd learn the new grader systems alongside the others when they come. And I'd keep the catering going for money and for something to do after I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the first picture where the timing works for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pastries on Saturdays, Viktor fixing the neighbours' cars, grandchildren on Sundays. Small things, but ours. Nothing owed to anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'who buys coffee'. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the mine had a bad year, nobody bought coffee, and our café died. A mine that runs itself doesn't stop for a flat white. That's the town's worry, not mine, but I'd still feel it.

S4.say: This one's fine for people my age and a warning for the young ones. The young ones should learn the new systems early.
S4.think: Ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview. My worry would be the town after we're gone, because if the mine runs itself, who buys coffee?
S4.do: Clears the café loan in the first three years, then saves for retirement. Learns new grader systems alongside colleagues when they come and keeps the catering going for money and for something to do later.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's the first picture where the timing works for them.
S4.quote: Ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview.
S4.fieldNote: With the long timeline Amira expects to retire well before robots come and is calm for the first time in the AGI pictures. Her concern turns outward to the town's economy, shaped by watching her café die in a downturn. Her plan is the same steady debt-then-savings path.

steps.text: Clear the café loan in three years, then save for retirement
Keep the weekend catering going into retirement
Keep grading roads at Mount Selwyn and learn new systems with the crew

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the robots would take Viktor's van and my grader in the same year, before my pension, and we might still owe the bank. What would help is the government letting people over fifty-five freeze business debts if they lose their jobs to automation, and a bit of help to start something small, like my catering. Practical help, not speeches.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the mine had a bad year, my café died. If the mine goes, every café, every hairdresser, every school goes with it. People forget that.

headlineQuote: When the mine had a bad year, my café died. If the mine goes, every café, every hairdresser, every school goes with it.
portrait: Amira Ziegler is 58 and grades the haul roads at the Mount Selwyn iron ore mine, a job she took nearly four years ago after the café she ran with her partner Viktor failed in a mining downturn. They still owe the bank for the café, have about two weeks of savings, and Viktor now drives a delivery van. She is careful, practical and good with money, calm in a plateau and anxious in steady change, when her first step is to restart weekend catering. AGI by 2028 alarms her because robots would take her grader and Viktor's van in the same year, 2031, before her pension, so she'd race to clear the loan and get on the council's list early. With five or ten years the robots arrive around or after her retirement, and she has a debt plan with real numbers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because robots would take her grader and her partner's delivery van in the same year, before her pension and possibly while they still owe the bank.
whatWouldHelp: Letting older workers who lose their jobs to automation freeze business debts, and help to start something small like her catering.
